item.title: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
item.description: Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as UN-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: GENEVA — Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as UN-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years. Scores of countries ended the weeklong UN conference on weapons by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn’t commit to binding rules sought by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries and activists. The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts as major military powers jockey for dominance. It also marked the latest failure to set guardrails for AI, at a time when some experts have warned about such systems breaking out of human control and going rogue. Izumi Nakamitsu, the UN high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year. Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language. Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounted to “pushing the can down the road for two more years.” They noted that most countries supported work toward a new treaty. Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: “States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities.” Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short. “Technology is moving faster than diplomacy,” said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. “Diplomats are very slow.” A call for speedy work and alternative routes toward a deal Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, had set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems. The UN’s Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work as early as Monday and “start thinking about how to get as strong as possible instrument to prohibit and regulate lethal autonomous weapon systems.” The International Committee of the Red Cross highlighted how autonomous weapons can be “unpredictable” — unlike, say, a bullet fired from a gun with a distinct and predictable trajectory. “For years, the ICRC and many others have urged states to ensure that humans retain control over the use of force and that life-and-death decisions are never handed over to machines,” it said in a statement. Advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism at this week’s talks largely by Russia, which, like other leading developers of AI weapons, including the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons. Pope Leo XIV and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily. Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened. Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and any deal is likely to be based on the lowest common denominator. Jamey Keaten, The Associated Press

item.title: A 10% drop for the stock market is unnerving, but it's not that unusual
item.description: The U.S. stock market has dropped 10 per cent from its high set last month amid concerns about the growing hurdles faced by the high-flying artificial intelligence industry.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: The U.S. stock market has dropped 10 per cent from its high set last month amid concerns about the growing hurdles faced by the high-flying artificial intelligence industry. The fall for the S&P 500 is steep enough that Wall Street has a name for it: a “correction.” Such drops have happened regularly for more than a century, and market pros often view them as potentially healthy wipeouts of overdone euphoria, which could send stock prices too high if unchecked. But corrections are unnerving in the moment. And the larger fear always accompanying a correction is that it could be a warning sign of a coming “bear market,” which is what Wall Street calls a drop of at least 20 per cent. Here’s a look at what history shows about past corrections, and what market watchers are expecting going forward. What’s behind this correction? Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence boom drove the markets to all-time highs in October. But a confluence of events caused investors to question whether the enthusiasm is overblown and if the AI industry can deliver on the lofty expectations. For one, investors are worried that stock prices in AI companies shot too high and that the strong demand for memory, processors and other building blocks of data centers could fizzle out if AI proves less profitable than promised. The large sums needed to invest in technology and data centers are another concern. The industry is racing to develop more capable models and infrastructure, which requires billions of dollars, but increasingly companies are having to raise money by selling bonds to investors. Now, the Federal Reserve is expected to hike its short-term interest rate next month. That could drive up borrowing costs for AI companies, among others. More recently, investors have grown anxious about the regulatory environment under a new Congress. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, elected Democratic governors who have vowed to stop new construction. Then there’s Nvidia. The company’s chips power the AI industry and it also provides the cash that’s helped companies across the industry to grow. The sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder, has punished the company’s stock and been a big factor in the broader sell-off. “Jensen Huang’s departure may have been the catalyst for this sell-off, but the underlying concerns in the technology sector have been building for some time,” said Karan Ramchandani, managing partner at Post Oak Group. “Investors have poured enormous amounts of capital into AI based on expectations of transformational growth, and we’re now entering a period where those expectations need to translate into measurable earnings and returns.” Not even the blockbuster market debut of AI lab Anthropic this week could stem the selling. Was there a tech bubble? And has it burst? Given their lofty valuations, Wall Street has been anticipating a correction in AI stocks for a while. Some who’ve referred to the run-up in the stocks a bubble think it hasn’t popped completely. “The bubble is popping and it has much further to go,” said David Trainer, head of investment research firm New Constructs. “We’re in the early innings of reconciliation with economic reality of egregious over-investment in AI. Like all other booms, this one is having its bust.” Others see the sell-off as another instance of the fear and anxiety that periodically grips the markets. Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., likened the current downturn to market corrections in March 2020 around the pandemic and in April 2025 following the Trump administration’s escalation of its global trade war. But he sees the selling as panic-driven, and not a “red flag moment indicating darker times ahead for tech and the market.” “This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting this 4th Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years,” Ives wrote. “And that is the wrong move in our view.” Ramchandani sees the sell-off as more of a reevaluation of the AI sector than the bursting of a bubble. “AI isn’t going away,” she said, “but the market may be entering a phase where investors become far more selective about which companies can actually deliver on the promises.” Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, says the washout being led by AI stocks could ultimately prove constructive for the broader market. “If this evolves into a true flush, it may serve as the reset needed to improve positioning, sentiment, and the odds of a more sustainable rally into year-end,” he said, in a research note. How often do corrections occur? Every couple years, on average. Even during the historic, nearly 11-year-long bull market for U.S. stocks from March 2009 to February 2020, the S&P 500 stumbled to five corrections, according to research firm CFRA. Worries about everything from interest rates to trade wars to a European debt crisis caused the pullbacks. The U.S. market’s last correction was in March 2025. The last correction that did graduate into a bear market was in 2022. Through the 2022 bear market, the S&P 500 fell 25.4 per cent from Jan. 3 to Oct. 12. What typically happens after a drop like this? Looking at the 25 corrections since 1946 that managed to right themselves before turning into a bear market, the S&P 500 has taken an average of 130 days to hit bottom and lost an average of nearly 14.1 per cent along the way, according to CFRA. The index has taken an average of 112 days to recoup its losses. For the 14 declines that became bear markets, the damage is much worse. Going back to 1946, the average bear market has caused a loss of 32 per cent for the S&P 500, according to CFRA. ___ Alex Veiga, The Associated Press Business Writers Bernard Condon, Kaitlyn Huamani and Damian Troise contributed.

item.title: Bay du Nord deepwater oil project clears final regulatory hurdle from Canada and N.L.
item.description: A proposal for Canada’s first deepwater oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle as the Newfoundland and Labrador government awaits the owner’s next move.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: ST. JOHN’S -- A proposal for Canada’s first deepwater oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle as the Newfoundland and Labrador government awaits the owner’s next move. Canada and Newfoundland and Labrador’s joint energy regulator approved Equinor’s development plan for Bay du Nord earlier this month. On Friday, officials from both governments gathered in St. John’s, N.L., to say they’d accepted that approval. All that’s left now is for Equinor to make a final decision to proceed with the $14-billion venture, and that decision is expected early next year, said Premier Tony Wakeham. And though climate scientists are urging governments to turn away from fossil fuels, the Newfoundland and Labrador government hopes Bay du Nord won’t be the last oil and gas development in its territory offshore. “We are talking to companies and countries all over the world who have an interest in coming here,” Lloyd Parrott, the provincial energy minister, told reporters. “We do things different than they do in the rest of the world, and we do things better.” The federal government approved Bay du Nord in the spring of 2022, but Equinor still had to submit its development plan to the joint Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator for scrutiny. The Norway-based company submitted the plan in May, and it was approved by Nov. 4, according to the province. Friday’s announcement about Bay du Nord came as a United Nations climate summit -- known as COP31 -- began to wrap up in Turkey. This year’s talks came amid urgent warnings that the planet is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures. The Quebec government also pledged at the summit to create a road map to transition away from fossil fuels as part of its membership in the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance -- a group of states and governments collaborating to phase out oil and gas production. Joanne Thompson, the federal fisheries minister, said Canada is working to build up clean energy resources, but traditional energy sources -- such as oil and gas -- are needed in the meantime. “This is how we control our destiny, how we are able to work toward our goal, but understanding that we need at this point to still have both conventional and clean energy,” she told reporters in St. John’s. Bay du Nord would be the first deepwater oil development in Canada, and farther from shore than any other oil project on Earth. Equinor would drill wells more than a kilometre below the surface of the ocean, in waters about 500 kilometres northeast of St. John’s. The company expects to extract more than 400 million barrels of oil, with first oil expected in 2031. Equinor is the majority owner and operator of Bay du Nord. British oil giant Shell recently announced it was buying a 30-per-cent share of the project and the Newfoundland and Labrador government is considering purchasing a 10-per-cent stake. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026. With files from The Associated Press
